There is an unmet clinical need for objective biomarkers to monitor disease progression and treatment response in Huntington’s disease (HD). The aim of this review is, therefore, to provide practical advice for biomarker discovery and to summarise studies on biofluid markers for HD. A PubMed search was performed to review literature with regard to candidate saliva, urine, blood and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers for HD. Information has been organised into tables to allow a pragmatic approach to the discussion of the evidence and generation of practical recommendations for future studies. Many of the markers published converge on metabolic and inflammatory pathways, although changes in other analytes representing antioxidant and growth factor pathways have also been found. The most promising markers reflect neuronal and glial degeneration, particularly neurofilament light chain. International collaboration to standardise assays and study protocols, as well as to recruit sufficiently large cohorts, will facilitate future biomarker discovery and development. Keywords Huntington’s disease biomarker blood plasma serum cerebrospinal fluid urine saliva INTRODUCTION Huntington’s disease (HD) is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG triplet repeat expansion in the gene encoding huntingtin [ 1 ]. HD is clinically characterised by a variable phenotypic expression of motor, cognitive and psychiatric symptoms [ 2 ], with typical age-at-onset in the thirties or forties [ 3 ] and a slow disease progression [ 4 ]. The age-at-onset, severity and duration of disease are very variable and depend on CAG repeat length as well as other genetic and environmental factors [ 3 ]. Although many clinical features of HD can be ascribed to the dysfunction and death of neurons, the causative mutant huntingtin protein is expressed ubiquitously and evidence is emerging of a role for non-neuronal tissues in the pathogenesis of HD [ 5–7 ]. Biomarker definition The term biomarker is defined as “a characteristic that is objectively measured and evaluated as an indicator of normal biological processes, pathogenic processes, or pharmacologic responses to a therapeutic intervention” [ 8 ]. Therefore, a biomarker can be related to the disease itself or to a treatment effect. Various biomarker categories are defined in Table 1 (based on BEST (Biomarkers, EndpointS, and other Tools) Resource [ 9 ]). An ideal disease biomarker should be closely linked to pathophysiology, reliable, accurate, sensitive, specific, reproducible, inexpensive, non-invasive and acceptable for the patient [ 10 ]. Huntington’s disease biomarkers: Unmet needs At present there are no effective treatments in clinical practice that will prevent the disease, halt its progression or delay its onset [ 11–13 ], but as the future holds promise for disease modifying strategies [ 14 ], there is a need for reliably assessable disease progression biomarkers, as well as markers to evaluate therapeutic interventions. As a chronic progressive disorder, HD has a premanifest phase during which no motor signs are present, but the underlying pathological processes are ongoing [ 15, 16 ]. The possibility of genetic testing in HD opens up the possibility of evaluating disease-modifying treatments already in the premanifest phase. Thus, biomarkers that reflect underlying disease processes or progression are needed to monitor changes in clinically asymptomatic individuals [ 17 ]. Biomarkers providing an objective measurement for the assessment of HD severity would also be valuable in the clinical care of existing HD patients and might prove particularly useful in a clinical trial context, potentially serving as surrogate endpoints. In 2004, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) emphasised the importance of biomarkers in improving drug development efficiency [ 18 ] and continues to promote research on potential new biomarkers to use as surrogates in future trials [ 19 ]. Since then, there has been an increase in the use of biomarkers in all phases of drug development. Impaired proteasome activity [ 20 ], transcriptional dysregulation [ 21 ], oxidative stress [ 22 ], mitochondrial and metabolic dysfunction [ 23 ], neuroinflammation [ 24, 25 ], and microglial activation [ 26–28 ] have been shown to play important roles in the pathogenesis of HD and many biomarker studies have been undertaken that reflect these processes (clinical, imaging and biofluid). Although much data has been generated, the road to clinical application is long and validation of the intended use in independent cohorts is challenging. To help identify the most promising candidate biomarkers, we reviewed “wet biomarker” literature in HD published to date. Here, we are defining a “wet biomarker” as a potential biomarker that is objectively measured in a bodily fluid. We have limited our focus to studies in blood, urine, saliva and CSF and have excluded DNA, RNA and microRNA studies. While these studies are also of great interest, they require a different set of criteria from markers discussed here and are beyond the scope of this review. We have built our discussion around a table giving an overview of wet biomarker studies to date. The supplementary table is an unbiased summary including all studies regardless of methodology and reproducibility, describing the markers evaluated, the number of subjects, disease stage and the main finding of the study. At the outset, our intention was to also include a table showing “validated” wet biomarkers that have been consistently reproduced and validated longitudinally; however, only one of the markers reviewed here met these criteria. None of the studies to date have yielded biomarkers for accurately predicting either age at onset or disease progression for HD. Since the first step towards clinical implementation of a newly discovered biomarker is independent replication, we focus on biomarkers that have been validated in at least two independent cohorts and we discuss recent data challenging earlier findings. The goal of this critical review is to highlight the most promising markers for future validation studies and to help investigators design future biomarker studies in HD.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Huntington's disease pathogenesis, including inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, endocrine system dysregulation, neuronal/glial degeneration, oxidative stress, and circadian rhythmicity.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Huntington's disease (HD) involves multifaceted pathological changes, including impaired proteasome activity, transcriptional dysregulation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial and metabolic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and microglial activation. Both innate and adaptive immune systems contribute to HD pathology, leading to a peripheral immune response, where proinflammatory cytokines like IL-6 induce acute-phase proteins and activate the complement cascade. Neopterin indicates cellular immune system activation. HD is associated with a negative energy balance and catabolic changes in amino acid metabolism, often preceding symptom onset. Alterations in cholesterol metabolites like 24(S) hydroxycholesterol reflect progressive neuronal loss, paralleling caudate volume reduction. Progressive neuronal death in the hypothalamus affects pituitary axes, leading to abnormal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis hyperactivity and somatotropic axis dysfunction. Impairment in the electron transport chain and mitochondrial dysfunction are major sources of increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and oxidative stress. Pathological changes affecting glial and neuronal brain tissue result in the release of proteins into CSF and blood. Circadian rhythmicity of analytes (cytokines, hormones, melatonin) can significantly impact measured levels. Untargeted 'omics' approaches offer a comprehensive biomarker fingerprint and insights into fundamental HD mechanisms.
related_biomarkers: Multiple molecules from genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics panels

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: No specific dose-response effect or comparison between high vs. low intensity/stage for biomarkers is consistently discussed, but several markers show stage-dependent changes. Immune changes, specifically increased IL-6, are apparent even during the preclinical stage of HD. Neopterin levels are consistently increased in late stages, but early-stage follow-up studies are lacking. Metabolic alterations, particularly catabolic changes in amino acid metabolism, are found in premanifest and early stage HD. One study indicated a reduction in total, HDL, and LDL-cholesterol in both premanifest and manifest HD subjects. Melatonin alterations are found in premanifest and stage II/III HD. HPA axis hyperactivity is reported in early disease (premanifest), with elevated salivary cortisol awakening response (CAR) in premanifest HD mutation carriers compared to diagnosed HD, and higher morning cortisol levels in premanifest versus symptomatic HD subjects. Morning fasting GH levels are higher in stage I/II HD, and increased somatotropic activity is associated with disease severity. Plasma lipid peroxidation products correlate with the degree of severity in HD patients. CSF mutant huntingtin (mtHTT) is increased in manifest HD CSF compared to premanifest HD CSF. A significant limitation across studies is the heterogeneity in patient cohorts regarding disease stage, making comparisons challenging.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: Biomarker specificity is a critical concern. While desired, many proposed markers for HD are criticized for being non-specific or variable, potentially reflecting general illness rather than HD-specific pathology. The increase in C-reactive protein (CRP) in HD mutation carriers may be confounded by antipsychotic use. Single time-point measures for hormones like melatonin and cortisol are insufficient to capture dynamic range or circadian rhythmicity, leading to conflicting results also attributed to varied biofluids, inconsistent confounder adjustment, and inappropriate control groups. Plasma neurofilament light protein (NF-L) is recognized for reflecting CNS pathology, making it particularly useful for trials targeting the CNS. 8-hydroxy-2-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) was initially promising but its validity is now questioned due to failed replication, high biological variability, and confounding factors such as stress, depression, smoking, diet, and pollution. Some analytes, despite not differing significantly between HD and control cohorts, may still correlate with specific disease measures.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Individuals with Huntington's disease (HD), including those in the premanifest phase (clinically asymptomatic), existing HD patients across early to late stages, HD mutation carriers, and symptomatic HD subjects.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: There is an unmet clinical need for objective biomarkers to monitor disease progression, evaluate therapeutic interventions, assess disease-modifying treatments, and determine HD severity. Inflammatory and metabolic markers can track HD progression, even in preclinical stages, with catabolic changes in amino acid metabolism occurring before symptom onset. Reduction of 24(S) hydroxycholesterol may reflect progressive neuronal loss. Alterations in pituitary axes, HPA axis hyperactivity, somatotropic axis dysfunction, energy metabolism, and oxidative stress contribute to HD pathology and potentially to early depressive symptoms. Biomarkers such as NF-L, T-tau, YKL-40, and mtHTT correlate with clinical measures, disease onset, and brain atrophy, indicating their potential for tracking progression and aiding in drug assessment. Lipid peroxidation products correlate with disease severity. Ultimately, biomarkers are crucial for improving the efficacy, duration, cost-effectiveness, and statistical power of HD clinical trials, facilitating patient stratification, accelerating drug development, and providing objective, quantitative endpoints for therapeutic response.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Biomarkers offer significant diagnostic utility for HD onset and progression, enabling early detection and understanding of pathogenesis, though many markers face criticism for lack of specificity and variability. They also serve as prognostic indicators for neuronal loss, disease progression, severity, and brain atrophy. HPA axis alterations pose an adverse risk, potentially contributing to depressive symptoms in early HD. Furthermore, these biomarkers hold promise as pharmacodynamic markers for therapeutic trials, potentially serving as surrogate endpoints to assess treatment effects.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The reliability of wet biomarkers for Huntington's disease (HD) is a major challenge. Validation of intended use in independent cohorts is difficult, with very few consistently reproduced or longitudinally validated biomarkers identified (only one met criteria in this review). No biomarkers have yet accurately predicted age at onset or disease progression. Inconsistencies abound, with mixed findings for IL-6 and CRP (often influenced by confounders like antipsychotic use). Neopterin shows consistent increase in late stages but lacks early-stage data. Branched chain amino acids show correlations but also reports of no change. While 24(S) hydroxycholesterol reduction is consistent, the validity of markers like 8-OHdG is questioned due to failed replication and high biological variability. Many conflicting studies are attributed to varied methodological factors, including underpowered studies (often less than 20 subjects per group), significant biological variation (intra- and inter-individual), predictable biological rhythms (daily, monthly, seasonally), and numerous confounding factors (age, activity levels, medication, gender, diet, ethnicity, smoking, alcohol consumption). Preanalytical variables (e.g., time of day, anticoagulant, feeding state, stress, sample storage/duration, blood collection tubes, processing duration) heavily influence reported analyte levels. The measurement of BDNF is particularly difficult due to its instability and sensitivity to preparation and individual factors. The lack of standardized/harmonized assays for novel biomarkers leads to non-comparable results across studies. A significant limitation is the prevalence of cross-sectional studies, hindering the examination of biomarker changes over time, and publication bias further skews perceived reliability, as negative results are less likely to be published. Currently, no biofluid biomarkers are fully validated as outcome parameters for HD.
recommended_alternatives: Standardize assays and study protocols, including rigorous SOPs for sample collection, processing, storage, and transport in multi-centre studies (e.g., TRACK-HD, EURO-HD network approaches).
Recruit sufficiently large, well-characterized, and balanced cohorts to minimize uncontrolled covariates.
Conduct longitudinal studies to examine biomarker changes over time and the rate of change as disease progresses.

Examine 24-hour profiles for dynamic markers like melatonin and cortisol, rather than single time-point measures, or explore alternative measures like cortisol levels in hair for longer-term exposure.
Study multiple pathways and endocrine markers in association to identify patterns of changes correlating with HD progression.
Utilize an integrated, multi-omics approach (genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics) to generate a comprehensive biomarker fingerprint.
Implement systems biology approaches, combining wet biomarker, experimental, clinical, and imaging data for a holistic understanding.
Prioritize international collaboration and standardization of biomarker studies and biobanking procedures.
Promote the publication of all data, including negative results, to provide a complete picture of biomarker research outcomes.
For protein analyses, plasma is recommended over serum due to higher intrinsic stability.
Split samples into multiple aliquots for analytes with freeze-thaw instability (e.g., cytokines).
Further investigate promising glial-related inflammatory CSF biomarkers such as YKL-40, GFAP, MCP-1, and sCD14.
Further investigate cytoskeletal and myelin markers of neurodegeneration, including NF-L, T-Tau, P-Tau181, MBP, NSE, and UCHL1.
